name: Counts for a histogram
brief:
A histogram of returns needs a count per bin. `edges` lists $k + 1$ increasing numbers, which make $k$ bins. Bin `i` holds the returns `x` with `edges[i] <= x < edges[i + 1]`, except that the last bin also holds a return equal to `edges[-1]`. A return outside the edges is not counted. This is the rule `ax.hist` uses.

Write `bin_counts(rets, edges)`.

Example. For `rets = [-0.015, 0.0, 0.004, 0.01, 0.02, 0.031]` and `edges = [-0.02, -0.01, 0.0, 0.01, 0.02]` the answer is `[1, 0, 2, 2]`: 0.02 sits on the last edge and counts, and 0.031 is outside.
constraints: All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Skip a return below `edges[0]` or above `edges[-1]` first. A return equal to `edges[-1]` goes in the last bin; any other is found by testing the bins in turn.

examples.note: 0.0 opens the third bin and 0.01 opens the fourth. 0.02 is the last edge, so it counts in the last bin.
One bin, closed at both ends. 2.0 is outside.

tests.call: (lambda c: (sum(c), c[:3], c[-3:]))(bin_counts([((i * 37) % 201 - 100) / 1000 for i in range(10000)], [j / 100 - 0.1 for j in range(21)]))

how: Submit runs 11 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Every bin is closed on the left and open on the right, and only the last bin is closed on both sides.
Testing `edges[i] < x <= edges[i + 1]` moves every return on an edge into the bin below, and drops one equal to `edges[0]`.
Testing each bin in turn is $O(nk)$; `bisect` on the edges makes it $O(n \log k)$.

planted.slip: Every bin is open on the right, so a return equal to the last edge is lost.
The bins are closed on the right instead of the left.
Returns outside the edges are pushed into the end bins instead of dropped.
